replying_to: Replying to Reference-Limited Compositional Learning: A Realistic Assessment for Human-level Compositional Generalization
display_title: Official Review of Paper2567 by Reviewer nsvK

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose a new task - Reference-Limited Compositional Learning, a corresponding benchmark and a baseline method. The task is a combination of compositional object + attribute recognition [Misra et al., CVPR'17] and few-shot image classification. In particular, they posit that it is unrealistic to expect that a learning system would have access to a large dataset of all possible object and attribute combinations at training time, and propose a more realistic scenario in which a mode is given only a few object-attribute pairs for training and has to learn to recognize not only these exact combinations, but also any other combinations of the same objects and attributes (i.e. training set might include red wine and green tomato, but at test time red tomato needs to be recognized). 

The benchmark consists of two parts, one focused on objects + attributes and another on objects + actions. Both are constructed by combining existing datasets.

The method is an extension of prototypical networks with a channel attention block that presumably allows to better disentangle object and attribute features during training.
content.main_review:
The paper is not very well written, though readable. In particular, there are virtually no illustrations making it hard to understand the details of the benchmark and the approach. 

While the proposed task and benchmark are valid and novel to the best of my knowledge, I find that they will be of little interest for the community. The problem of compositional recognition is challenging and under explored even in the non-few-shot regime, so I doubt that any real progress will be made in the more challenging few-shot setting in the near future. This is evident from the fact that all the evaluated methods show an extremely low performance on novel attribute-object combinations on the proposed benchmarks.

The baseline approach is also a combination of existing methods and the improvements over vanilla Prototypical Networks are not statistically significant or barely statistically significant, depending on the setting.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed task and benchmark are novel to the best of my knowledge, however, they are simply a combination of two existing tasks and several existing datasets respectively. I don't think this constitutes a valuable contribution for the reasons stated above. That said, strictly speaking, all the boxes are checked (novel task + benchmark, a baseline that provides some minimal improvements over existing methods), so there are no formal reasons for rejection aside from the sub-par presentation. I will leave the decision to AC's judgement.

content.title: Response to Reviewer nsvK
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and suggestions. We have updated the paper and below are our responses.

> The paper is not very well written, though readable. In particular, there are virtually no illustrations making it hard to understand the details of the benchmark and the approach.

Thanks for the suggestion. We have added an illustration of how to apply the approaches on our RLCL task to the updated paper. And we have also made textual improvements to the paper, which we hope will help the readers understand the paper in more depth.

> While the proposed task and benchmark are valid and novel to the best of my knowledge, I find that they will be of little interest for the community. The problem of compositional recognition is challenging and under explored even in the non-few-shot regime, so I doubt that any real progress will be made in the more challenging few-shot setting in the near future. This is evident from the fact that all the evaluated methods show an extremely low performance on novel attribute-object combinations on the proposed benchmarks.

First of all, we are glad to see that all the reviewers, including you, agree that our proposed RLCL is a novel and valuable task. We give the following reasons to explain why our work will stimulate the research interest of the community:

1. Recently the two topics of few-shot learning and compositional learning have attracted more attention, with an ocean of efforts emerging and various leaderboards being refreshed. However, at the intersection of these two areas, we propose that there are limitations to the current concerns, which makes them somewhat distant from real-world scenarios.
2. One of the very important contributions of our paper is that we built a realistic platform for AI systems to simulate how humans learn in a compositional manner when encountering various new environments. This is valuable for further research on how to endow AI systems with human-level generalization ability.
3. In the initial development phase of such a new task, the unsatisfied performance of baselines adapted from existing methods cannot indicate that real progress will fail to be made. Instead, what it indicates is that the problem is unexplored and remains a wide scope for exploration.
4. In addition, taking into account the comments of all the reviews, we have relaxed the restrictions on side information. This allows us to further update our approach while adding the state-of-the-art CZSL methods to the comparison, leading to a significant improvement in the best performance on the benchmark.

According to the above discussion, we believe that now is an appropriate time to start the discussion on this task, and our work can serve as a strong foothold for future studies.

> The baseline approach is also a combination of existing methods and the improvements over vanilla Prototypical Networks are not statistically significant or barely statistically significant, depending on the setting.

As we have stated in the paper, the original version of our proposed refined-ProtoNet is just ''a competitive baseline that must be considered for defeat in future studies''. However, we think it is hard to say that the improvements ''are not statistically significant or barely statistically significant'', since there was a (7.89 - 4.25) / 4.25 = **86%** increase of HM on RLCL-ATTR and a (6.55 - 5.17) / 5/17 = **27%** increase on HM on RLCL-ACT with default settings. Such improvements indicate that rather than simply combining existing methods, we are indeed looking for a right way to more effectively separate the visual features corresponding to the semantic primitives from the compositions, which is quite challenging under the constraints of both few-shot and few referential compositions. Moreover, after deciding to introduce side information, we have updated our refined-ProtoNet, which currently has a uniform form and can be transformed depending on the availability of side information. By using side information as class descriptions, our approach has achieved more significant improvements, and we provide the results (UA / SA / HM) here for your reference:

|       | RLCL-ATTR | RLCL-ACT |
| :---        | :----: | :---: |
| vanilla ProtoNet | 2.23 / **45.97** / 4.25 | 2.75 / **44.89** / 5.17 |
| refined-ProtoNet (**w/o** side information) | 4.36 / 42.03 / 7.89 | 3.60 / 36.92 / 6.55 |
| refined-ProtoNet (**with** side information) | **6.05** / 39.31 / **10.48** | **6.18** / 32.04 / **10.35** |

Considering that a high SA coupled with a low HM somewhat reflects the degree of overfitting, we believe that our updated refined-ProtoNet does have its distinct contributions on the RLCL task as it better meets the goal of identifying compositions including seen and unseen ones.

replying_to: Replying to Reference-Limited Compositional Learning: A Realistic Assessment for Human-level Compositional Generalization
display_title: Official Review of Paper2567 by Reviewer nYmZ

content.summary_of_the_paper: The article describes the problem of Reference Limited Compositional Learning (RLCL), where the goal is to recognize compositions of primitives (e.g. attributes-objects, actions-objects) given a few examples depicting them.  The query images may contain both seen and unseen compositions of the support primitives. To address this task, a refined version of ProtoNet (Snell et al. 2017) is proposed, where the input features are filtered through an attention mechanism. Experiments on two proposed benchmarks show that refined-ProtoNet surpasses the performance of various few-shot baselines and a simple compositional zero-shot learning one (CZSL).
content.main_review:
**Strengths**:
1. The paper presents an interesting problem setup, where a model should recognize possibly unseen compositions of primitives at test time, given a few examples. This problem formulation merges the challenges of few-shot learning, CZSL, and generalized zero-shot learning, since the model could be inherently biased toward support compositions. The low performance achieved by all models (e.g. below 5% on unseen composition recognition) demonstrates that the problem is very challenging.
2. The proposed RLCL-attr and RLCL-act benchmarks encompass various compositional datasets and may serve as a future, interesting benchmark for the community, also in CZSL.
3. Related works and the introduction are comprehensive and well written, perfectly explaining the contribution of the work.

**Weaknesses**:
1. The first weakness is the technical contribution. The proposed refined-ProtoNet is not a method tailored for the RLCL task, but rather an additional baseline built on the combination of existing techniques (the term baseline is also used to define the approach at the end of Section 4.2). As acknowledged in Section 4.2, refined-ProtoNet combines the original ProtoNet with the CBAM attention module of (Woo et al. 2018). This is also similar to what other few-shot baselines have done in the past (e.g. [a] with CrossTransformers) and there are no justifications on why the attention module promotes the higher accuracy on unseen compositions, shown in Table 1. A more solid method, addressing all the challenges of RLCL would have strengthened the contribution of the manuscript, showing the need for a tailored approach to tackle this task. 
2. While it is true that most recent CZSL techniques assume the presence of side information describing the category of interest, it is also true that Table 1 tests on RLCL only a single CZSL method, VisProd, the very first baseline for this task (Nagarajan &
Grauman, 2018). A thorough benchmark would have included more recent CZSL methods (e.g. Atzmon et al. 2020, Naeem et al. 2021, [b]) and, possibly, coupling them with existing few-shot learning techniques. For instance, an easy comparison would have been instantiating the side information used by these recent methods through ProtoNet-based class weights. Including more recent baselines and naive combinations of few-shot and CZSL ones would have contributed, as for the previous point, to stress the need for specific methods addressing the RLCL problem.

References:  
[a] Doersch, Carl, Ankush Gupta, and Andrew Zisserman. "Crosstransformers: spatially-aware few-shot transfer." NeuriPS 2020.  
[b] Li, Yong-Lu, et al. "Symmetry and group in attribute-object compositions." CVPR 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: I find the problem presented in the manuscript very interesting and worth studying. However, the proposed method is not tailored to the proposed task and the experimental comparisons do not include recent CZSL baselines (eventually combined with few-shot learning approaches naively). For these reasons, I lean toward a negative rating.

content.title: Response to Reviewer nYmZ
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful comments. We have updated the paper and below are our responses.

> The proposed refined-ProtoNet is not a method tailored for the RLCL task, but rather an additional baseline built on the combination of existing techniques.

Although we have stated in the paper that the original version of our proposed refined-ProtoNet is just ''a competitive baseline that must be considered for defeat in future studies'', this does not mean that it is not a method tailored for the RLCL task. The empirical performance of all baselines, including newly added CZSL methods (please refer to the next Q&A), has indicated that effectively separating the visual features corresponding to the specific semantic primitives, either explicitly or implicitly, is quite challenging under the constraints of both few-shot and few referential compositions. We believe that designing a simple but efficient architecture to do this better has its own task-specific contribution to the RLCL task, and can provide inspiration for subsequent studies. Moreover, after deciding to introduce side information, we have updated our refined-ProtoNet, which currently has a uniform form and can be transformed depending on the availability of side information (please refer to Section 3.2 of the updated paper for more details). Therefore, it can no longer be seen as a combination of existing methods. Taking further performance improvements into account, we believe that our proposed approach does have its distinct contributions on the RLCL task.

> Including more recent baselines and naive combinations of few-shot and CZSL ones would have contributed, as for the previous point, to stress the need for specific methods addressing the RLCL problem.

Thanks for the suggestion. Firstly, after discussing the comments from all the reviews, we decide to relax the restrictions on side information and include the results of two state-of-the-art CZSL methods, SymNet[1] and CGE[2], in our paper. The reported results using pre-trained word2vec or Glove word embeddings as label embeddings, *i.e.*, class descriptions. We believe that the addition of these two methods can demonstrate the performance that the best CZSL methods can achieve on our RLCL task, although we also plan to include more recent CZSL methods in our next version of the paper. 

We also agree that under the constraint that side information is not available, replacing the above class descriptions with class prototypes yields reasonable baselines. We have completed experiments on this and here we report the main results of SymNet, CGE and our proposed refined-ProtoNet when using different class descriptions:

**RLCL-ATTR** (UA / SA / HM):

|       | word2vec | Glove | prototypes |
| :---        | :----: | :---: | :---: |
| SymNet | 1.96 / 18.47 / 3.54 | 2.45 / 18.24 / 4.32 | 3.11 / 14.80 / 5.14 |
| CGE | 4.65 / 15.40 / 7.13 | 4.27 / 16.37 / 6.77 | 1.75 / 21.81 / 3.24 |
| refined-ProtoNet | **6.05** / **39.31** / **10.48** | **5.14** / **39.76** / **9.10** | **4.36** / **42.03** / **7.89** |

**RLCL-ACT** (UA / SA / HM):

|       | word2vec | Glove | prototypes |
| :---        | :----: | :---: | :---: |
| SymNet | 2.96 / 17.12 / 5.04 | 3.72 / 16.12 / 6.04 | **4.06** / 14.95 / 6.38 |
| CGE | 4.05 / 15.51 / 6.41 | 2.76 / 18.81 / 4.80 | 2.36 / 22.99 / 4.27 |
| refined-ProtoNet | **6.18** / **32.04** / **10.35** | **6.05** / **35.93** / **10.34** | 3.60 / **36.92** / **6.55** |

These results show that our refined-ProtoNet outperforms state-of-the-art CZSL methods. More results and discussions have been included in Section 4 and Appendix G of the updated paper.

[1] Symmetry and group in attribute-object compositions, CVPR 2020.

[2] Learning Graph Embeddings for Compositional Zero-shot Learning, CVPR 2021.

content.title: Thanks for the response
content.comment:
I thank the authors for their detailed response. However, I tend to keep my original rating. 

The reason is that, despite the new task being interesting, the paper is not demonstrating its necessity well enough in its current version. In particular, proposing a new task should also entail that it needs to be addressed with specific solutions. In the current version of the manuscript, I find this aspect missing since:

- While adding CGE and SymNet strengthens the experimental comparisons, the experiments do not report results of baselines combining CZSL approaches with FSL ones (e.g. even the simpler VisProd, LabelEmbed + ProtoNet, or MAML). Showing that these baselines are not effective (or they underperform a tailored, proposed method) is the first step in demonstrating the need for specific solutions for the new task. 

- The proposed approach combines ProtoNet (on primitives) with the attention maps of CBAM. The compositional aspect of the problem is mainly treated through the separation of prototypes per primitives (rather than compositional class). The fact that the problem can be addressed by separating primitives and applying existing techniques, does not support well the need for defining a new task. Adding side information does not contribute in this direction, since it is not linked to the compositionally of the problem. 

I think the task is interesting and the paper has the potential to provide an interesting compositionality benchmark for the computer vision community. However, for the above-mentioned reasons, I tend toward maintaining my original score for the current version of the manuscript.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2567 by Reviewer mn6T

content.title: Response to Reviewer mn6T
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments and suggestions. We have updated the paper and below are our responses.

> Why were the benchmarks splits defined so that the train and test samples are very different datasets? Could this be enough to justify the bad performance of all methods on the task?

The reason why we define the current splits is that the size of existing datasets cannot support us to select train and test samples from the same dataset. Our proposed RLCL task requires not only the data and compositions, but also the primitives from train and test splits should be non-overlapping. This results in a very limited number of primitives and compositions contained in each split. Therefore, when we tried to select both train and test splits from the same dataset, we found that the train split was too small to satisfy adequate training. More importantly, the test split with few primitives and compositions could not be used to construct a large number of diverse testing episodes, making the evaluation of methods unconvincing. This reason was briefly explained and we have now updated Section 2.3 to explain it in more detail.

Considering that domain gaps may be introduced due to inconsistent data sources, selecting splits from multiple datasets instead of the same dataset naturally makes this task more difficult. However, inspired by the cross-domain few-shot learning topic which is developed from conventional FSL, we believe that such domain gap should be considered to overcome by future studies. As the goal of our RLCL is to become a realistic assessment for human-level compositional generalization ability, the domain gap also tests whether AI systems can truly adapt and reason as quickly as humans to new environments that are completely different from previous ones. In addition, based on comments from other reviews, we have increased the number of baselines and improved our proposed method, resulting in a significant improvement in the best performance on this task. This shows that such domain gap does not overshadow the impact of other challenges and the progress that should be made by various methods. In summary, we believe that the current setup about splits will not negatively impact the overall goal of the RLCL task.

> How many classes were considered? Reporting accuracy without the number of classes can be misleading. 

As discussed in Problem Formulation, our RLCL task applies an episodic manner as well as an open world setting to evaluate methods. In each test episode, the number of compositional pairs as prediction candidates is related to the number of each type of primitive $N^p$ in the episode. For example, in our default setting, $N^p$=5, so the prediction space contains 5 * 5 = 25 possible compositional pairs, including seen compositions, unseen compositions and compositions that do not actually exist in the dataset. Note that we impose no constraint on the test time search space, unlike the commonly used evaluation setting in CZSL. We have updated Section 2.1 to make it more explicitly stated in the paper.

> The explanation in figure 1 is not quite clear, adding an explanation of what is happening in the "Realistic scenario" side could help. More examples of what are primitives and of how the RLCL task differs from established tasks would also be helpful.

Thank you for the suggestion. We have made changes to the paper, including but not limited to the title of Figure 1 and Introduction, to make the motivation for the RLCL task clearer.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new compositional learning setup where the reference for the compositions is subject to low supervision. While humans seem to be able to solve the problem, it can be a challenging task for the existing learning algorithms. The paper looks into this problem and proposes new benchmarks and baseline results.
content.main_review:
**Strengths**

- I agree it is an interesting problem to consider the case of limited reference.
- The authors put several existing datasets together to create new datasets for RLCL.

**Weaknesses**

- Many recent works in Compositional Zero-Shot Learning and Few-Shot Learning are not considered in the related works and experiments. Some examples of missing related works:

Memory-Augmented Relation Network for Few-Shot Learning, ACM Multimedia 2020
Dynamic Few-Shot Visual Learning without Forgetting, CVPR 2018
Embedding Propagation: Smoother Manifold for Few-Shot Classification, ECCV 2020

Given missing references to those recent works, it is hard to claim that ProtoNet is indeed a competitive method in the literature and the proposed refined-ProtoNet is a strong baseline, because some recent models may prove to be better. We don't have a clear understanding of the state of the art from the current experiments.

- It is strange to see the claim "Such semantic descriptions of classes are difficult to collect in the real-world environment" although those descriptions are available in the other CZSL datasets and they have been broadly used in the literature. At the same time, the discussion of baseline methods for CZSL cases is very limited.

- refined-ProtoNet uses a beefed-up network without proposing new ideas. As we can improve any model by adding new components borrowed from the representation learning literature, it is not clear what we can learn from this model.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the proposed question is interesting, I found the discussion of the related works and claim about the new base model is problematic. It is not clear what is our current progress on the proposed problem, therefore I am leaning towards rejection.

Please refer to the next Q&A for more details about it. However, for FSL, while we have added a discussion of more recent works in the section of Related Work, these works cannot be easily extended to our proposed RLCL task. First, many methods rely on elaborate arithmetic and structural designs, and establishing a parallel classification branch for each primitive type would result in doubling the number of parameters and computation time. Moreover, we also experimented with some methods in advance, such as FEAT[1], and their performance was similar to random prediction, showing that they struggled with highly entangled image representations. Therefore, we believe that the current selected baselines are sufficient as a starting point for the study of the RLCL problem, and how to make uncovered recent FSL methods available for RLCL with non-trivial extensions could be left to follow-up studies.
